scope: Neutral-only USB 0x10 transport timing; no motor parameters, no configuration command

runs.note: Every write failed with 'USB output did not complete within 4ms': the worker thread inherited the 4 ms default bound, so written=0 and the low lateness was vacuous.

findings: Back-to-back neutral writes complete every ~8 ms (cadence median 8.003 ms, min 6.908, max 8.138), so the 8 ms is the endpoint polling interval, not Windows API overhead.
The controller's OUT endpoint therefore accepts about 125 frames per second; an 8 ms haptic frame period matches the hardware exactly.
A synchronous writer on an 8 ms grid leaves zero margin (one write = one period); with a 4 ms grid it accumulates about 4 ms of lateness per frame.

Overlapping the blocking write with the dispatcher removes the problem: on an 8 ms grid, dispatch lateness is 0.0026 / 0.3237 / 0.5439 ms (min/median/max), 0 frames over 4 ms, and 32/32 frames written with 0 replaced.

Two separate 4 ms bounds produced false results in this campaign: the diagnostic's dispatch guard (stopped the run) and the writer's default timeout (rejected every write). Both are now explicit: 50 ms transport bound, lateness recorded not fatal.
Lateness in the synchronous grid run (0.0065 -> 91.08 ms) is accumulation of ~4 ms per frame, a property of the serial loop, not of the device.
limits: WriteFile completion is not controller ACK and says nothing about haptics.
Endpoint bInterval is inferred from cadence, not read from the descriptor.
Frames were neutral; the overlapped writer has not yet carried a real haptic frame.
One host, USB direct to the machine, two short sessions.
next: Carry a real haptic frame through the overlapped writer on the 8 ms grid, then compare what the controller actually produces against the requested waveform.
